atomic: Imagine surviving an atomic bomb... only to be caught in another one, three days later.
August 1945. Engineer [Tsutomu](/tsutˈOmu/) [Yamaguchi](/jˌɑməɡˈuʧi/) is finishing a three-month work trip in Hiroshima.
On the morning of August sixth, he walks back toward the shipyard.
At eight fifteen... a blinding flash.
About three kilometres away, the blast throws him down and burns his upper body.
The next day, bandaged and exhausted, he takes a train home... to Nagasaki.
On August ninth, he's back at work, describing the bomb to his boss.
Then the room fills with white light.
A second atomic bomb has exploded over Nagasaki.
In 2009, Japan officially recognised [Tsutomu](/tsutˈOmu/) [Yamaguchi](/jˌɑməɡˈuʧi/) as a survivor of both bombings.
He lived to ninety-three, speaking out against nuclear weapons.
Two atomic bombs. One survivor. And he spent his life warning the world.
strato: This man stepped off a platform nearly thirty-nine kilometres above Earth.
Felix [Baumgartner](/bˈWmɡɑɹtnəɹ/) rides a pressurised capsule beneath a giant helium balloon.
For over two hours, it climbs into the stratosphere, above ninety-nine percent of the atmosphere.
The sky turns black. The horizon curves.
He opens the door... and steps onto the ledge.
In air this thin, nothing slows him down. Within thirty-four seconds, he breaks the speed of sound.
Then he starts to spin. Faster. And faster.
A spin like this could knock him unconscious.
After four minutes and nineteen seconds of freefall, his parachute opens.
Minutes later, he lands on his feet in the desert.
Top speed: Mach one point two five, over thirteen hundred kilometres an hour.
No engine. No aircraft. Just one man, falling faster than sound.
alcatraz: The guards thought these prisoners were asleep. But the heads in their beds were fake.
June eleventh, 1962. Alcatraz, the island prison in San Francisco Bay.
The dummy heads were made from soap, toilet paper and real human hair.
For months, Frank Morris and brothers John and Clarence Anglin had been digging.
With sharpened spoons and a drill made from a vacuum motor, they widened the air vents behind their sinks.
Painted fake grilles hid the holes.
That night, they crawled into a dark utility corridor, climbed the pipes to the roof...
...and slipped down to the water's edge.
There, they inflated a raft made from more than fifty stolen raincoats.
Around ten p.m., they pushed off into the cold, black water.
By morning, guards found only dummies in the beds.
More than sixty years later, what happened to them remains unknown.
